name: Calendula cream

lead: Calendula cream is a topical product made from the orange and yellow flowers of Calendula officinalis, the pot marigold. It is sold as a soothing skin cream, and calendula extracts are widely used in cosmetics.

People use it for dry, irritated or sensitive skin and for minor skin reactions, so that skin looks calmer and less red. Research includes trials in radiation skin reactions, with mixed results, and a small 2025 trial in irritant contact dermatitis that measured skin hydration and barrier recovery.

paras: The cream is applied to the skin like a regular moisturiser or soothing balm, often to irritated, dry or reddened areas. It is also found as an ingredient in baby, sensitive-skin and natural-skincare lines. Users generally describe it as part of a gentle routine rather than a treatment with a fixed schedule.

Calendula belongs to the daisy family (Asteraceae), and people sensitive to related plants can develop contact reactions. In trials, side effects were generally minor. Cream applied during radiotherapy should be discussed with the treating team, since trials in that setting have compared calendula with other creams rather than replacing medical care.

chain: Calendula extract applied in a cream
Soothes irritated skin and supports hydration and barrier recovery
angle.text: Calendula cream is used as a soothing moisturiser for dry or irritated skin. In a small controlled forearm study, skin treated with a calendula emollient was better hydrated and recovered barrier function faster than comparison sites.

lead: Calendula cream is a topical preparation containing extract or oil of Calendula officinalis (pot marigold), a daisy-family plant whose flowers have long been used in traditional medicine and as a colourant for foods and cosmetics [1]. It is sold as a soothing moisturiser and is common in sensitive-skin and baby-care products.

For appearance, people use it to calm redness and dryness and to support the skin barrier so skin looks and feels smoother. A small randomized trial of an emollient with and without a 1 percent supercritical CO2 calendula extract found greater skin hydration at the calendula-treated sites than at untreated or base-cream sites after an irritant challenge [2].
Larger trials have studied calendula cream mainly to prevent radiation skin reactions in cancer patients, with mixed results [3][4][5].

paras: Calendula officinalis is a short-lived aromatic herb up to about 80 cm tall with yellow or orange flowerheads, probably native to southern Europe and widely naturalised [1]. Its flowers contain carotenoids and triterpenoid compounds, and flower oil and extracts are widely used in skin products [1].

Traditionally, leaves and flowers were used as poultices for scratches and shallow cuts, and in ancient Greek, Roman, Middle Eastern and Indian cultures the plant served as a medicinal herb and as a dye [1].

Calendula creams are marketed for dry, sensitive and irritated skin, including baby skin. They are used to restore comfort and reduce visible redness, and often appear in natural and gentle skincare lines [1].
Laboratory studies of calendula extracts have reported anti-inflammatory, antibacterial and antifungal activity, which proponents cite as the rationale [1].

A 2025 double-blind trial in 20 healthy volunteers tested a base emollient with and without 1 percent calendula CO2 extract on irritant-exposed forearm sites. Hydration was significantly higher at the calendula site than at control and placebo sites on day 4, and persisted to day 8; transepidermal water loss was lower than at control on day 3 [2].

In radiotherapy, a 2013 randomized blinded trial of 420 breast cancer patients compared a calendula cream with an aqueous cream and found no difference in severe acute radiation skin reactions (23 percent versus 19 percent) [3]. A review of radiation skin care noted limited early evidence that calendula might reduce grade 2 and 3 reactions in breast cancer, while concluding evidence was insufficient to recommend specific agents [4]. A 2025 randomized trial in head and neck cancer compared the Chinese herbal ointment Bao Yuan Gao with calendula cream; severe dermatitis rates did not differ, though Bao Yuan Gao reduced erythema and improved moisture at week 3 [5].
Calendula is a member of the daisy family, and contact sensitivity can occur in people allergic to related plants. Trials in radiotherapy reported the creams as generally tolerated [3].
